SEM Fit and Model Comparison: Definitions, Uncertainty, and Use

Ken Kelley

November 2026

Source: vignettes/sem_fit_measures.Rmd
sem_fit_measures.Rmd

A structural equation model claims that the covariances of the observed variables (and, with a mean structure, their means) follow from a smaller set of parameters. Judging the fit of the model asks how well that claim holds, and the question has four parts that are easy to run together, each answered by different evidence.

  1. Exact fit. Does the model reproduce the population moments exactly? The chi square test answers this question, and with a large sample it rejects nearly every model, because nearly every model is an approximation.
  2. The size of the misfit. If the model is an approximation, how far is it from the population, and how precisely do the data say so? The root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) and the standardized root mean square residual (SRMR) are effect sizes of misfit, and each is reported here with a confidence interval and the tests that interval implies.
  3. Improvement over a baseline. How much of the misfit of a model that explains nothing does the model remove? The incremental indices (CFI, TLI, and their relatives) answer this question relative to a baseline model, which the researcher should name.
  4. Choice among models. Which of several candidate models do the data favor, and by how much? Information criteria and the expected cross-validation index rank models fitted to the same data.
Function What it reports Input
sem_fit_measures() The chi square test; the RMSEA with its interval and the tests of close and not close fit; CFI, TLI, NFI, IFI, and RNI; the SRMR; gamma hat and adjusted gamma hat with their intervals A fitted lavaan model, or the statistics a paper reports
equivalence_rmsea() The test that the population RMSEA is below a bound chosen in advance, with its interval and verdict The statistics a paper reports
sem_residual_fit() The SRMR, its unbiased estimate with an interval, tests of exact and close fit, and the largest standardized residual A fitted lavaan model
sem_information_criteria() AIC, BIC, SABIC, HBIC, IBIC, and SPBIC of one model A fitted lavaan model, or its log likelihood and parameter count
compare_sem() Models ranked by one criterion, with differences, weights, and approximate log Bayes factors Fitted lavaan models
ci_rmsea(), ecvi() An interval from a reported RMSEA; the expected cross-validation index with its interval A reported value, or a fitted model

Two conventions run through all of them. Misfit is treated as a population quantity to be estimated with an interval, not as a verdict read off a cutoff, so the intervals and the tests they imply come first. And each function returns one table of one shape whatever its arguments: a row that a setting does not compute is present and NA, so that code that reads a row by its name keeps working. The models are fitted with lavaan (Rosseel, 2012), which must be installed to run the code below.

The Running Example

Holzinger and Swineford (1939) gave 26 ability tests to the seventh and eighth grade pupils of two Chicago schools, and holzinger_swineford holds the scores of all 301 pupils. Jöreskog (1969) illustrated his general approach to confirmatory maximum likelihood factor analysis with nine of the tests, which he took to measure visualization (visual perception, cubes, and lozenges), verbal intelligence (paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning), and speed (addition, counting dots, and straight and curved capitals), in the 145 pupils of the Grant-White school. The analysis here uses the same nine tests in both schools, and the substantive question is the one Jöreskog asked: do three correlated abilities account for the covariances among the nine tests?

library(DMAR)
tests <- c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges",
           "t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence", "t9_word_meaning",
           "t10_addition", "t12_counting_groups_of_dots",
           "t13_straight_and_curved_capitals")
d <- descriptives(holzinger_swineford[tests])$descriptives
print(d[, c("variable", "n", "mean", "sd", "skewness", "kurtosis")],
      digits = 3)
#>                           variable   n   mean    sd skewness kurtosis
#> 1             t1_visual_perception 301  29.61  7.00   -0.257    0.355
#> 2                         t2_cubes 301  24.35  4.71    0.475    0.381
#> 3                      t4_lozenges 301  18.00  9.05    0.387   -0.888
#> 4       t6_paragraph_comprehension 301   9.18  3.49    0.270    0.123
#> 5                      t7_sentence 301  17.36  5.16   -0.353   -0.525
#> 6                  t9_word_meaning 301  15.30  7.67    0.867    0.876
#> 7                     t10_addition 301  96.28 25.06    0.252   -0.274
#> 8      t12_counting_groups_of_dots 301 110.54 20.25    0.531    1.240
#> 9 t13_straight_and_curved_capitals 301 193.47 36.33    0.206    0.337

The tests are scored in their original units, with standard deviations from 3.49 to 36.33. The fit measures do not depend on the units of the variables, but one of the information criteria does, and the point returns in its section. Skewness and excess kurtosis are modest, the largest in absolute value being 0.87 and 1.24.

The model has three correlated factors. Each is identified by fixing its variance at 1 (std.lv = TRUE), so that every loading is estimated and the covariances among the factors are correlations.

three <- "
  visual =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges
  verbal =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning
  speed  =~ t10_addition + t12_counting_groups_of_dots +
            t13_straight_and_curved_capitals
"
fit_three <- lavaan::cfa(three, data = holzinger_swineford, std.lv = TRUE)

# One or more values of a DMAR table, by the names of their rows.
v <- function(x, term) x$value[match(term, x$term)]

The Discrepancy and the Test Statistic

For pp observed variables with population covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol\Sigma, the model expresses the covariances as functions of a parameter vector 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta. For the factor model above,

𝚺(𝛉)=𝚲𝚽𝚲′+𝚯, \boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)= \boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi\boldsymbol\Lambda'+\boldsymbol\Theta,

with 𝚲\boldsymbol\Lambda the loadings, 𝚽\boldsymbol\Phi the factor correlations, and 𝚯\boldsymbol\Theta the diagonal matrix of unique variances (Jöreskog, 1969). Maximum likelihood (ML) estimation under multivariate normality minimizes the discrepancy

FML{𝐒,𝚺(𝛉)}=log⁡|𝚺(𝛉)|+tr⁡{𝐒𝚺(𝛉)−1}−log⁡|𝐒|−p, F_{ML}\{\mathbf S,\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)\}= \log|\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)|+ \operatorname{tr}\{\mathbf S\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}\} -\log|\mathbf S|-p,

which is zero only when the model implied covariance matrix equals the sample covariance matrix 𝐒\mathbf S (a model with a mean structure adds a term for the means). Write F̂\hat F for the minimum and F0F_0 for the minimum the model would reach if it were fitted to the population covariance matrix, the population discrepancy. The test statistic is T=aF̂T=a\,\hat F for a sample size multiplier aa. Under lavaan’s default normal likelihood, TT is the likelihood ratio statistic of the model against the saturated model, T=2(ℓs−ℓM)=NF̂T=2(\ell_s-\ell_M)=N\hat F, so that a=Na=N. The literature on which the RMSEA and its interval were built forms TT with the unbiased covariance matrix and a=N−1a=N-1 (Browne & Cudeck, 1993; MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996), and with GG groups each group contributes its size less one, a=N−Ga=N-G (Steiger, 1998). The degrees of freedom are the number of sample moments less the number of free parameters, here 9×10/2=459\times 10/2=45 variances and covariances less 21 parameters, so dfdf = 24.

When the model holds exactly, TT is approximately chi square on dfdf degrees of freedom. When the model is wrong by an amount that is not large relative to sampling error, TT is approximately noncentral chi square with noncentrality λ=aF0\lambda=a\,F_0 (Browne & Cudeck, 1993; MacCallum et al., 1996). Every measure below that rests on λ\lambda (the RMSEA, its interval, the tests of close and not close fit, gamma hat, and the ECVI) needs the multiplier with which TT was formed, a point taken up in its own section.

Version: standard (auto: a normal theory ML fit of complete data with no corrected statistic)

Chi square: standard

The lines under the table say which version of the measures was reported and why (the standard version, for a normal theory fit of complete data; see the section on versions) and with what multiplier the statistic was formed. Every value from chi_square through srmr equals the one lavaan reports for the same fit (lavaan’s default bound for not close fit is .08, which not_close_fit = 0.08 reproduces). Gamma hat and its limits are the index lavaan calls gfi_lrt, which it reports only when asked for it by name; the gfi lavaan prints by default is computed from Browne’s residual based statistic instead, and adjusted gamma hat has no lavaan counterpart (the agfi lavaan gives when asked is the sample adjusted GFI of LISREL).

Exact Fit

The first three rows test exact fit, H0:F0=0H_0:F_0=0, by the upper tail of the central chi square distribution at TT: χ2\chi^2(24) = 85.31, pp < 0.0001. Exact fit is rejected. With 301 pupils that result says little on its own: a test of exact fit has power against any misfit when the sample is large, and a small sample can fail to reject a poor model. A model with zero degrees of freedom reproduces the sample moments by construction and has no test; its pp-value, RMSEA, interval, tests of close and not close fit, and TLI are NA, with a warning that says so. Its statistic is zero in every version, so its CFI is 1 in every version too, and its RNI, NFI, and IFI are their values at a statistic of zero.

The RMSEA and Its Interval

The RMSEA, introduced by Steiger and Lind (1980) in a presentation whose handout Steiger (2016) reproduces, is the population discrepancy per degree of freedom on the scale of a square root (Browne & Cudeck, 1993):

ε=F0/df,ε̂=Gmax⁡(T−df,0)adf. \varepsilon=\sqrt{F_0/df},\qquad \hat\varepsilon=\sqrt{\frac{G\max(T-df,\,0)}{a\,df}}.

Because E(T)≈df+λE(T)\approx df+\lambda, T−dfT-df estimates λ\lambda, and a negative estimate is truncated at zero. Steiger (2000) shows that the truncated estimate is to be preferred to the untruncated one under what he calls the primacy principle, and that the tests and the interval are computed from TT itself, not from the truncated estimate, so the truncation discards nothing they use. The factor GG is the number of groups, 1 here.

The interval inverts the noncentral chi square distribution at the observed TT: the lower limit for λ\lambda is the noncentrality that puts TT at the upper α/2\alpha/2 quantile of χdf2(λ)\chi^2_{df}(\lambda), the upper limit is the one that puts it at the lower α/2\alpha/2 quantile, and both are mapped to the RMSEA metric in the same way as the estimate (ci_nc_chisq() does the inversion). When TT lies at or below the upper α/2\alpha/2 quantile of the central distribution, no positive noncentrality reaches the lower limit and it is 0. When TT lies at or below the lower α/2\alpha/2 quantile, no noncentrality is consistent with TT at that level, and the upper limit is reported as 0, as lavaan reports it and as Yuan, Chan, Marcoulides, and Bentler (2016) define the corresponding T-size RMSEA (below); the printed footer then says so.

For the three-factor model ε̂\hat\varepsilon = 0.092, 90% CI [0.071, 0.114]. The interval carries what the estimate cannot: the population RMSEA is plausibly as small as 0.071 or as large as 0.114, and that width is the precision 301 cases buy for a model with 24 degrees of freedom. ss_aipe_rmsea() plans the sample size that makes the expected width of the interval as narrow as a study needs (Kelley & Lai, 2011).

The RMSEA is conventionally reported with a 90% interval (Browne & Cudeck, 1993), the one lavaan prints, and the reason is that a 100(1−2α)%100(1-2\alpha)\% interval decides the two one-sided tests at level α\alpha described next (MacCallum et al., 1996, p. 136), so the two limits of a 90% interval are those tests at .05. That is why every RMSEA interval in DMAR, and the SRMR interval of sem_residual_fit(), defaults to 90%, where the package’s other intervals default to 95%; the line beneath each table states the level. conf_level = 0.95 gives the 95% interval, [0.067, 0.118] here, whose limits decide the same tests at .025.

Tests of Close and Not Close Fit

Browne and Cudeck (1993) proposed testing close fit, H0:ε≤ε0H_0:\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0, in place of exact fit. Its pp-value is the upper tail P{χdf2(λ0)≥T}P\{\chi^2_{df}(\lambda_0)\ge T\}, with λ0=adfε02/G\lambda_0=a\,df\,\varepsilon_0^2/G the noncentrality at the bound. Rejecting close fit is evidence that the model does not fit closely; failing to reject it is not evidence that the model does. MacCallum et al. (1996) reversed the roles of the hypotheses. Their test of not close fit, H0:ε≥ε1H_0:\varepsilon\ge\varepsilon_1, takes the lower tail P{χdf2(λ1)≤T}P\{\chi^2_{df}(\lambda_1)\le T\} as its pp-value, and rejecting it supports fit within ε1\varepsilon_1. The two tests and the interval are one piece of evidence seen three ways: at level .05, close fit is rejected exactly when the lower limit of the 90% interval exceeds ε0\varepsilon_0, and not close fit is rejected exactly when the upper limit falls below ε1\varepsilon_1 (MacCallum et al., 1996, Table 1).

Both bounds default to .05, the value MacCallum et al. (1996) used for both; lavaan’s default bound for not close fit is .08, which not_close_fit = 0.08 reproduces. The bounds frame a test; they do not certify a model, and Steiger (1998) cautions that cutoff values such as .05 may not survive careful scrutiny as rules for adequacy. For the three-factor model, close fit within .05 is rejected (pp = 0.0007), as the lower limit 0.071 above .05 implies, and not close fit is not rejected (pp = 0.9993).

Fit Within a Tolerance Chosen in Advance

The test of not close fit is an equivalence test (Yuan et al., 2016): it endorses a model whose misfit is below a tolerance, rather than merely failing to reject it. equivalence_rmsea() reports it with its interval and a verdict. The tolerance must be chosen before the data are seen and justified by the use to which the model will be put; there is no universal value. Suppose the investigators had decided in advance that a population RMSEA below .08 would make the three-factor model a tolerable approximation for their purpose.

equivalence_three <- equivalence_rmsea(chisq = v(fit_measures, "chi_square"),
                                       df = v(fit_measures, "df"), N = 301,
                                       rmsea_bound = 0.08,
                                       sample_size_convention = "N")
equivalence_three

ci_lower 0.071
ci_upper 0.114
rmsea_bound 0.080
null_noncentrality 46.234
p_value 0.8396
equivalent 0

Not close fit (RMSEA >= 0.08) is not rejected at alpha = 0.05: fit within the bound is not established (upper limit 0.114), which is not evidence of poor fit.

Sample size: N = 301 in 1 group; multiplier a = 301 (sample_size_convention = “N”)

The statistic was formed by lavaan under its default likelihood, so the call passes sample_size_convention = "N". Not close fit is not rejected (pp = 0.8396): fit within .08 is not established, which is a different conclusion from showing that the fit is poor. The upper limit, 0.114, is the T-size RMSEA of Yuan et al. (2016, Eq. 4): the data endorse the model at α=.05\alpha=.05 for every bound above it, which makes it the number to report when no bound was fixed in advance. Yuan et al. form TT with N−1N-1, the default of the function.

The Sample Size Convention

A fitted model carries its own multiplier. lavaan forms TT with NN for ML under its default normal likelihood, and with N−GN-G under likelihood = "wishart" and for the least squares estimators; sem_fit_measures() reads the multiplier from the fit, which is why its values match lavaan’s. Statistics copied from a paper carry no such record, so the summary statistic input of sem_fit_measures(), equivalence_rmsea(), and ci_rmsea() takes sample_size_convention, with the default "N-1". That is the convention of Browne and Cudeck (1993), of MacCallum et al. (1996), of Kelley and Lai (2011), and of DMAR’s ss_aipe_rmsea() and ss_power_sem(). lavaan’s default likelihood and Mplus form TT with NN, so statistics taken from their output take "N".

fm <- lavaan::fitMeasures(fit_three)
summary_input <- function(convention) {
  sem_fit_measures(chisq = fm[["chisq"]], df = fm[["df"]], N = 301,
                   baseline_chisq = fm[["baseline.chisq"]],
                   baseline_df = fm[["baseline.df"]], p = 9,
                   sample_size_convention = convention)
}
rows <- c("rmsea", "rmsea_ci_lower", "rmsea_ci_upper", "p_close_fit",
          "gamma_hat")
print(data.frame(row = rows, fitted = v(fit_measures, rows),
                 summary_N = v(summary_input("N"), rows),
                 summary_N_minus_1 = v(summary_input("N-1"), rows)),
      digits = 4)
#>              row    fitted summary_N summary_N_minus_1
#> 1          rmsea 0.0921215 0.0921215         0.0922749
#> 2 rmsea_ci_lower 0.0714185 0.0714185         0.0715374
#> 3 rmsea_ci_upper 0.1136780 0.1136780         0.1138673
#> 4    p_close_fit 0.0006612 0.0006612         0.0006479
#> 5      gamma_hat 0.9566992 0.9566992         0.9565611

With "N" the summary input reproduces the fitted values. The default "N-1" moves them in the fourth decimal place, a difference of order 1/N1/N that matters when a published value is to be reproduced and is the reason a report should state its convention. ci_rmsea() starts from a reported RMSEA instead of from TT; its default level is also 90%, and the call below names it:

ci_rmsea(rmsea = v(fit_measures, "rmsea"), df = 24, N = 301,
         conf_level = 0.90, sample_size_convention = "N")
term value
ci_lower 0.071
rmsea 0.092
ci_upper 0.114

Confidence level: 90%

It rebuilds T=adfε̂2+dfT=a\,df\,\hat\varepsilon^2+df, which recovers the statistic unless ε̂\hat\varepsilon was truncated at zero. Every TT at or below dfdf produces an estimate of zero, so for such a model the interval needs the chi square statistic itself, which sem_fit_measures() and equivalence_rmsea() take.

Several Groups

Holzinger and Swineford tested two schools so that the stability of their bifactor solution could be judged by fitting it in each. Fitting the three-factor model to both schools with nothing constrained to be equal across them (the configural model of an invariance analysis) gives one statistic on twice the degrees of freedom.

fit_schools <- lavaan::cfa(three, data = holzinger_swineford, std.lv = TRUE,
                           group = "school")
schools <- sem_fit_measures(fit_schools)
schools[schools$term %in% c("chi_square", "df", "rmsea", "rmsea_ci_lower",
                            "rmsea_ci_upper", "N", "n_groups"), ]
term value
chi_square 115.851
df 48
rmsea 0.097
rmsea_ci_lower 0.075
rmsea_ci_upper 0.120
N 301
n_groups 2

Confidence level: 90%

Version: standard (auto: a normal theory ML fit of complete data with no corrected statistic)

Chi square: standard

Sample size: N = 301 in 2 groups; multiplier a = 301 (lavaan’s normal likelihood forms T with N)

Steiger (1998) showed that the RMSEA of a model fitted to GG independent samples divides the overall discrepancy by the average degrees of freedom per group, ε=GF0/df\varepsilon=\sqrt{G F_0/df} (his Eq. 23), and that putting a multiple group statistic into the single group formula gives values too small by the factor G\sqrt G (his Eq. 25). A fitted model supplies GG, and summary input takes it as n_groups:

rmsea_rows <- c("rmsea", "rmsea_ci_lower", "rmsea_ci_upper")
from_summary <- function(groups) {
  v(sem_fit_measures(chisq = v(schools, "chi_square"),
                     df = v(schools, "df"), N = 301, n_groups = groups,
                     sample_size_convention = "N"),
    rmsea_rows)
}
print(data.frame(row = rmsea_rows, fitted = v(schools, rmsea_rows),
                 groups_2 = from_summary(2), groups_1 = from_summary(1)),
      digits = 4)
#>              row  fitted groups_2 groups_1
#> 1          rmsea 0.09691  0.09691  0.06853
#> 2 rmsea_ci_lower 0.07451  0.07451  0.05268
#> 3 rmsea_ci_upper 0.11958  0.11958  0.08456

Left at groups = 1, the summary input understates the RMSEA, 0.069 against 0.097, a ratio of 1.414, which is 2\sqrt 2. equivalence_rmsea() takes n_groups in the same way, with the same convention; ci_rmsea() assumes a single group.

Incremental Indices

The incremental indices compare the model’s statistic with that of a baseline model fitted to the same data, by default the independence model, in which the observed variables are uncorrelated. Writing TbT_b and dfbdf_b for the baseline statistic and its degrees of freedom,

CFI=1−max⁡(T−df,0)max⁡(T−df,Tb−dfb,0),RNI=1−T−dfTb−dfb,TLI=Tb/dfb−T/dfTb/dfb−1,NFI=Tb−TTb,IFI=Tb−TTb−df. \begin{aligned} CFI&=1-\frac{\max(T-df,\,0)}{\max(T-df,\,T_b-df_b,\,0)},& RNI&=1-\frac{T-df}{T_b-df_b},\\ TLI&=\frac{T_b/df_b-T/df}{T_b/df_b-1},& NFI&=\frac{T_b-T}{T_b},\qquad IFI=\frac{T_b-T}{T_b-df}. \end{aligned}

The comparative fit index is due to Bentler (1990), and without its truncation at zero it is the relative noncentrality index (Bentler, 1990; McDonald & Marsh, 1990). The Tucker-Lewis index (Tucker & Lewis, 1973) is also called the nonnormed fit index (Bentler & Bonett, 1980), who also proposed the normed fit index; the incremental fit index is due to Bollen (1989). Hu and Bentler (1998, Table 1) collect these definitions. No index is clipped to [0,1][0,1] (RNI and TLI can exceed 1), and an index whose denominator is zero or negative is NA.

Here the independence model has TbT_b = 918.85 on 36 degrees of freedom, and CFI = 0.931 and TLI = 0.896. CFI says that the model removes about 93% of the independence model’s estimated noncentrality. That is a statement relative to a model nobody believes, and the same model looks better against a worse baseline; van Laar and Braeken (2022) point out that the incremental indices are standardized effect sizes relative to the baseline, with the same limits on their interpretation and no universal rule of thumb. Brosseau-Liard and Savalei (2014) give the population values the sample indices estimate. None of the indices has a confidence interval here: the usual asymptotic theory assumes misfit small relative to sampling error, and the independence model is far from that.

Gamma Hat

Gamma hat (Steiger, 1989; Hu & Bentler, 1998, Table 1) rescales the estimated noncentrality to a goodness of fit metric that needs no baseline model, and adjusted gamma hat penalizes it for the degrees of freedom used. They estimate the population values of the goodness of fit index (GFI) and the adjusted GFI that LISREL reports, which Steiger (1989) showed to be these functions of the population noncentrality for a model invariant under a constant scaling factor (a result he restates in Steiger, 1990, p. 178):

γ̂=pp+2(T−df)/a,γ̂adj=1−p(p+1)2df(1−γ̂). \hat\gamma=\frac{p}{p+2(T-df)/a},\qquad \hat\gamma_{adj}=1-\frac{p(p+1)}{2\,df}\,(1-\hat\gamma).

Both can exceed 1 when T<dfT<df. Each is a monotone function of the noncentrality, so the limits of the noncentrality interval behind the RMSEA interval give their limits, p/(p+2λ/a)p/(p+2\lambda/a) at each limit λ\lambda (Steiger & Fouladi, 1997, pp. 251–252). For the three-factor model γ̂\hat\gamma = 0.957, 90% CI [0.936, 0.974], and γ̂adj\hat\gamma_{adj} = 0.919 [0.879, 0.950]. Steiger’s result is for covariance structures: the function computes the two indices for the standard version of a single group, single level ML fit of continuous variables without FIML or sampling weights, and for the robust version of such a fit by MLM, MLR, MLMV, or MLMVS, but not for a model that restricts the means (a growth model, say, or intercepts constrained equal, to a constant, or to another parameter, or held at the bound of an inequality constraint), whose statistic and degrees of freedom count mean restrictions that pp and p(p+1)/2p(p+1)/2 do not; free means change nothing. Whether a fitted model restricts its means is read from the derivatives of its moments, with the constraints that bind at the estimates imposed (its equality constraints, and the inequality constraints lavaan treats as active): the means are free when they add no degree of freedom. Summary input gives the two indices when p is given and df is at most p(p+1)/2p(p+1)/2; it carries no mean structure, so below that bound supplying p states that the model is a covariance structure. Elsewhere their rows are NA.

Standard, Scaled, and Robust Versions

The chi square statistic of a normal theory ML fit has its chi square distribution only under multivariate normality. The robust ML estimators (lavaan’s MLM and MLR) keep the ML estimates and correct the statistic for the nonnormality of the data. A fitted model can therefore carry more than one statistic, and each fit measure has a version for each:

  • standard: the measures computed from the uncorrected statistic, the right ones for a normal theory ML fit of complete continuous data;
  • scaled: the corrected statistic TsT_s on its degrees of freedom put in place of TT and dfdf in the standard formulas, for the RMSEA, its interval, and the tests of close and not close fit alike, the substitution EQS and Mplus report. lavaan’s default for a Satorra-Bentler or Yuan-Bentler statistic instead refers the unscaled TT to the noncentral chi square on c⋅dfc\cdot df degrees of freedom, for the scaling constant cc, which gives the same point estimate but another interval; sem_fit_measures() reports the substitution, which lavaan gives under rmsea.scaled.mplus = TRUE. Brosseau-Liard, Savalei, and Li (2012) showed that the RMSEA so computed estimates a quantity that decreases as nonnormality increases, not the population RMSEA, and Brosseau-Liard and Savalei (2014) made the same argument for CFI and TLI. The scaled version is offered to reproduce a published table;
  • robust: lavaan’s corrected measures, which estimate the population values of the standard measures. For a robust ML fit they are the correction of the RMSEA that Brosseau-Liard et al. (2012) recommend and that of Brosseau-Liard and Savalei (2014) for CFI, TLI, and RNI, with that of Savalei (2018) for a scaled and shifted statistic. Savalei (2018) shows that these do not depend on which corrected statistic accompanies them, so for the older mean and variance adjusted statistic (MLMVS), for which lavaan computes none, sem_fit_measures() computes them, and they equal lavaan’s for the same model fitted by MLM. For a ULS fit of continuous data, DMAR withholds the entire ML-derived robust family, including robust CFI, TLI, and RNI (Savalei, 2018). A common-units invariance check alone does not validate those corrections outside their derivation. Eligible scaled indices remain qualified diagnostics: they do not estimate the same population discrepancy as ML-based indices, and ML cutoffs do not automatically apply. Standard ULS indices that change with the units are withheld, and so are indices at mean-restricted rungs where the fit function combines squared mean and covariance residuals in different units. These restrictions also apply to the invariance ladder. A fit by ULS alone is tested by Browne’s residual based statistic, which has no units, and its measures are kept unless the model restricts the means through parameters the covariances share, as the scalar rung of an invariance ladder does through the loadings; the ULS estimates, and with them that statistic and its measures, then change with the units, and those measures are NA too. For ordered categorical data fitted by WLSMV they are those of Savalei (2021); and for a FIML fit they are the FIML corrected indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023). NFI and IFI have no robust version; the robust gamma hat is computed from the robust noncentrality and the robust RMSEA interval.

The default version = "auto" reports the robust version for a fit that carries a corrected statistic or uses FIML, and the standard version for a normal theory ML fit of complete data. Where lavaan has a corrected statistic but no robust measures, it reports, with a warning, the standard version of a continuous ML fit, whose standard measures estimate the population values the robust ones estimate and the scaled ones do not (Savalei, 2018), and the scaled version of any other fit. lavaan can compute Browne’s residual based statistic beside the standard one; it is an alternative test of exact fit, not a correction, and does not change the version reported. The sem_fit attribute and the printed footer name the version, the reason, and the statistic in the chi_square row.

fit_three_mlr <- lavaan::cfa(three, data = holzinger_swineford,
                             std.lv = TRUE, estimator = "MLR")
mlr_measures <- sem_fit_measures(fit_three_mlr)

The robust RMSEA is 0.092, 90% CI [0.072, 0.114]; the scaled RMSEA (version = "scaled") is 0.093 and the standard one 0.092. lavaan’s scaling factor for this fit is 0.98, close to 1, which is why the versions agree to two decimals here; with heavier tailed data they part, and only the robust one estimates the population RMSEA of the ML discrepancy.

Full Information Maximum Likelihood

Two of the 26 tests were given only at Grant-White. One of them, flags (t26_flags), is a spatial test, and adding it as a fourth indicator of the visual factor makes its scores missing by design for the 156 Pasteur pupils. Full information maximum likelihood (FIML; missing = "ml") uses every pupil’s observed scores.

The RMSEA and CFI that software has long reported after FIML are computed from the FIML statistic, and Zhang and Savalei (2023) review evidence that for a misspecified model their population values change with the amount of missing data, typically toward better fit as more data are missing. Their FIML corrected indices evaluate the complete data ML fit function at the FIML estimates, with the saturated FIML estimates of the means and covariances in place of the sample moments (their Eq. 11), and so approximate the RMSEA and CFI the model would have had with complete data. They are corrections for missing data, not for nonnormality, and the default reports them for every FIML fit, a plain ML one included; the chi_square row remains the FIML likelihood ratio statistic. Here the corrected RMSEA is 0.077 and CFI 0.943, against 0.079 and 0.935 for the uncorrected ones. Zhang and Savalei (2023) found that the correction can fail when a large share of the data is missing and the misspecification is severe. Whether the data are missing at random is a separate assumption that no fit index checks. Here the flags scores are missing because of the school a pupil attended, so FIML assumes that school carries no information about flags scores beyond what the other eight tests carry.

Ordered Categorical Data and Sampling Weights

For ordered categorical indicators fitted by WLSMV, the standard statistic is not chi square distributed, so the standard pp-value is NA and the default reports the corrected measures of Savalei (2021). A fit with sampling weights maximizes a weighted pseudo likelihood (Asparouhov, 2005), whose standard statistic is not chi square either, and the default reports lavaan’s robust measures. Requesting the standard version of either kind of fit, or the scaled version of an ordered categorical one, warns why it is not valid. Full WLS (estimator = "WLS") is the exception among the estimators for ordered data: its weight matrix is the inverse of the asymptotic covariance matrix of the thresholds and polychoric correlations, its statistic is asymptotically chi square (Browne, 1984; Muthén, 1984), lavaan reports its pp-value, and its standard measures are reported without a warning. The residual inference and the information criteria below are refused for both kinds of fit, for the reasons given in their sections.

Residual Fit

The SRMR and Its Unbiased Estimate

The SRMR summarizes the covariance residuals in the metric of a correlation (Bentler, 1995; Hu & Bentler, 1998, Table 1). With sample covariances sijs_{ij} and model implied covariances σ̂ij\hat\sigma_{ij},

eij=sij−σ̂ijsiisjj,SRMR=1t∑i≤jeij2,t=p(p+1)2. e_{ij}=\frac{s_{ij}-\hat\sigma_{ij}}{\sqrt{s_{ii}s_{jj}}},\qquad SRMR=\sqrt{\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i\le j}e_{ij}^2},\qquad t=\frac{p(p+1)}{2}.

A residual of .10 is a correlation the model misses by .10, which makes the SRMR easier to read than the RMSEA. Both sem_fit_measures() and sem_residual_fit() report this covariance definition; lavaan’s own srmr also averages in the mean residuals when a model has a mean structure, and sem_residual_fit() reports those separately as srmr_mean.

The sample SRMR overestimates its population value, since sampling error adds to every residual. Maydeu-Olivares (2017) removed the bias on the squared scale. With 𝐞\mathbf e the vector of standardized residuals and 𝚵̂\hat{\boldsymbol\Xi} their asymptotic covariance matrix, the unbiased estimate is

SRMR̂u=k̂−1max⁡(𝐞′𝐞−tr⁡𝚵̂,0)t,k̂=1−tr⁡(𝚵̂2)+2𝐞′𝚵̂𝐞4(𝐞′𝐞)2 \widehat{SRMR}_u=\hat k^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{\max(\mathbf e'\mathbf e-\operatorname{tr}\hat{\boldsymbol\Xi},\,0)}{t}}, \qquad \hat k=1-\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\hat{\boldsymbol\Xi}^2) +2\,\mathbf e'\hat{\boldsymbol\Xi}\mathbf e}{4(\mathbf e'\mathbf e)^2}

(Maydeu-Olivares, Shi, & Rosseel, 2018, Eq. 16). Its interval is the large sample normal interval SRMR̂u±z1−α/2SE\widehat{SRMR}_u\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,SE (their Eq. 20), reported as lavaan computes it, without truncation, so its lower limit can fall below zero, and when the estimate is truncated at zero the interval is centered at zero. The test of close fit, H0:SRMR≤cH_0:SRMR\le c (their Eq. 21), rejects at level α\alpha exactly when the lower limit of the 100(1−2α)%100(1-2\alpha)\% interval exceeds cc, so a 90% interval, the default of sem_residual_fit() as it is of the RMSEA functions, pairs with a test at .05. The test of exact fit uses the sample SRMR and its expected value and standard error under exact fit; the row srmr_se_exact_fit is that standard error, which holds only under exact fit and is not the one to build an interval from. In the simulations of Maydeu-Olivares et al. (2018), with 10 to 60 observed variables and normal and nonnormal data, the intervals and tests of close fit of the SRMR computed without assuming normality were generally accurate, whereas those of the RMSEA were accurate only in small models and, with 30 or more variables, wrongly suggested that models did not fit closely; the SRMR interval did worse than that of the RMSEA only when the misfit was very small in a model of 10 variables.

The bound cc is again the researcher’s choice. Shi, Maydeu-Olivares, and DiStefano (2018) proposed reference values that scale with the average R2R^2 of the observed variables (their average communality): close fit when the SRMR is at most .05R‾2.05\bar R^2 and the largest absolute standardized residual is at most .10, and acceptable fit at .10R‾2.10\bar R^2 and .15. They are population values, and Shi et al. (2018) recommend applying them through an interval or a test of close fit rather than to the sample values. Ximénez, Maydeu-Olivares, Shi, and Revuelta (2022) found the bound on the SRMR, applied to the unbiased SRMR, to work reasonably well in finite samples, except that with small loadings (an average R2R^2 of .09) close fit called for samples of 500 or more, and recommend it. sem_residual_fit() tests the first part; the second is read from the largest absolute residual, a sample value.

r2_three <- lavaan::lavInspect(fit_three, "rsquare")
residual_three <- sem_residual_fit(fit_three,
                                   close_fit = 0.05 * mean(r2_three))
residual_three

The average R2R^2 is 0.507, so the bound is 0.025. The unbiased SRMR is 0.058, 90% CI [0.042, 0.074], below the sample value 0.065, and close fit is rejected (pp = 0.0003). The largest absolute residual, 0.189, exceeds .10 as well, so by both parts of the criterion of Shi et al. (2018) the model does not fit closely. The residual covariance in the footer is normal theory, as the fit’s standard errors are. For an MLR or MLM fit it is asymptotically distribution free, the version to use with nonnormal data, for which Maydeu-Olivares et al. (2018) found the normal theory intervals to cover poorly. sem_residual_fit() covers ML and robust ML fits of one group of complete continuous data and refuses other fits (FIML, ordered indicators, several groups, sampling weights, among others) with a message that says why.

Reading the Residuals

An average can hide a concentrated failure, so the residuals themselves are worth reading. The test names are shortened to their numbers for display.

residuals_three <- attr(residual_three, "standardized_residuals")
dimnames(residuals_three) <- lapply(dimnames(residuals_three), sub,
                                    pattern = "_.*", replacement = "")
round(residuals_three, 2)
#>        t1    t2    t4    t6    t7    t9   t10   t12   t13
#> t1   0.00                                                
#> t2  -0.03  0.00                                          
#> t4  -0.01  0.09  0.00                                    
#> t6   0.07 -0.01 -0.07  0.00                              
#> t7  -0.01 -0.03 -0.15  0.01  0.00                        
#> t9   0.06  0.03 -0.03 -0.01  0.00  0.00                  
#> t10 -0.14 -0.19 -0.08  0.04 -0.04 -0.01  0.00            
#> t12 -0.04 -0.05 -0.01 -0.07 -0.04 -0.02  0.07  0.00      
#> t13  0.15  0.07  0.15  0.05  0.07  0.06 -0.04 -0.03  0.00

The largest residual, -0.19 between cubes and addition, says the model implies more covariance between those two tests than the data show. The more coherent pattern is in the row of straight and curved capitals (t13), a speed test whose residuals with all three visual tests are positive (0.15, 0.07, and 0.15): the model understates what that test shares with visualization. Telling straight capital letters from curved ones at speed plausibly draws on visual perception, which suggests letting the test load on the visual factor as well. A modification suggested by the residuals of the same data is exploratory, and the fit of the modified model is an optimistic estimate of how it would fit new data.

cross <- paste(three, "visual =~ t13_straight_and_curved_capitals",
               sep = "\n")
fit_cross <- lavaan::cfa(cross, data = holzinger_swineford, std.lv = TRUE)
cross_measures <- sem_fit_measures(fit_cross)
residual_cross <- sem_residual_fit(
  fit_cross,
  close_fit = 0.05 * mean(lavaan::lavInspect(fit_cross, "rsquare")))
equivalence_cross <- equivalence_rmsea(chisq = v(cross_measures, "chi_square"),
                                       df = v(cross_measures, "df"), N = 301,
                                       rmsea_bound = 0.08,
                                       sample_size_convention = "N")
fit_rows <- c("chi_square", "df", "rmsea", "rmsea_ci_lower",
              "rmsea_ci_upper", "cfi", "tli", "srmr")
residual_rows <- c("unbiased_srmr", "unbiased_srmr_ci_lower",
                   "unbiased_srmr_ci_upper", "largest_absolute_residual")
print(data.frame(row = c(fit_rows, residual_rows),
                 three_factor = c(v(fit_measures, fit_rows),
                                  v(residual_three, residual_rows)),
                 cross_loading = c(v(cross_measures, fit_rows),
                                   v(residual_cross, residual_rows))),
      digits = 3)
#>                          row three_factor cross_loading
#> 1                 chi_square      85.3055       52.3821
#> 2                         df      24.0000       23.0000
#> 3                      rmsea       0.0921        0.0651
#> 4             rmsea_ci_lower       0.0714        0.0418
#> 5             rmsea_ci_upper       0.1137        0.0886

Every measure moves toward better fit. The RMSEA interval of the cross-loading model, [0.042, 0.089], still reaches above .08, so the test of not close fit at the bound chosen earlier does not reject (pp = 0.1577), and the T-size RMSEA is 0.089. The unbiased SRMR, 0.035, 90% CI [0.020, 0.049], lies above the bound 0.026 for close fit of Shi et al. (2018), although the interval is too wide for the test of close fit to reject (pp = 0.1721), and the largest residual, 0.156, still exceeds .10. Whether the cross-loading model is to be preferred to the three-factor model is a question of comparison, taken up next.

Comparing Models

Information Criteria

An information criterion is minus twice the maximized log likelihood ℓ\ell plus a penalty for the dd free parameters; smaller values are preferred, and only a difference between models fitted to the same data under the same likelihood carries meaning. Bollen, Ray, Zavisca, and Harden (2012) derive the Bayesian members of the family from the Laplace approximation to the log of a model’s marginal likelihood,

log⁡P(Y∣M)=ℓ+log⁡P(𝛉̂∣M)+d2log⁡(2π)−d2log⁡N−12log⁡|𝐈‾E(𝛉̂)|+O(N−1/2) \log P(Y\mid M)=\ell+\log P(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\mid M) +\frac d2\log(2\pi)-\frac d2\log N -\frac12\log\bigl|\bar{\mathbf I}_E(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\bigr| +O(N^{-1/2})

(Bollen, Harden, Ray, & Zavisca, 2014, Eq. 9), where P(𝛉̂∣M)P(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\mid M) is the prior density at the estimates and 𝐈‾E\bar{\mathbf I}_E the expected information per observation. Multiplied by −2-2, the criteria keep different terms:

  • BIC=−2ℓ+dlog⁡NBIC=-2\ell+d\log N keeps the first and fourth terms (Schwarz, 1978);
  • HBIC=−2ℓ+dlog⁡{N/(2π)}HBIC=-2\ell+d\log\{N/(2\pi)\} keeps the third as well (Haughton, 1988);
  • IBIC=−2ℓ+dlog⁡{N/(2π)}+log⁡|𝐈‾E|IBIC=-2\ell+d\log\{N/(2\pi)\}+\log|\bar{\mathbf I}_E| keeps every term but the prior (Bollen et al., 2012, 2014);
  • SPBIC replaces the unit information prior of BIC with a normal prior centered at a prior mean 𝛉*\boldsymbol\theta^* whose variance, a multiple of the inverse unit information, is chosen to maximize the marginal likelihood (Bollen et al., 2012). With Q=(𝛉̂−𝛉*)′𝐈O(𝛉̂−𝛉*)Q=(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\boldsymbol\theta^*)'\mathbf I_O (\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\boldsymbol\theta^*) for the whole sample observed information 𝐈O\mathbf I_O, SPBIC=−2ℓ+d{1+log⁡(Q/d)}SPBIC=-2\ell+d\{1+\log(Q/d)\} (Bollen et al., 2014, Eq. 18). When Q≤dQ\le d the maximizing prior variance is zero, the prior is a point mass at 𝛉*\boldsymbol\theta^*, and SPBIC=−2ℓ+QSPBIC=-2\ell+Q; Bollen et al. (2014, note 7) never met that case and caution that its behavior is little known, and the function warns when it applies.

Two criteria rest on other arguments. AIC=−2ℓ+2dAIC=-2\ell+2d (Akaike, 1974) estimates the relative expected Kullback-Leibler discrepancy between a model and the process that generated the data (Burnham & Anderson, 2004). SABIC=−2ℓ+dlog⁡{(N+2)/24}SABIC=-2\ell+d\log\{(N+2)/24\}, the sample size adjusted BIC (lavaan’s bic2), has a penalty that Sclove (1987) presents among the criteria descended from Rissanen’s principle of the shortest data description. In the simulations of Lin, Huang, and Weng (2017), which selected among path models, SPBIC and HBIC did best across most conditions, SABIC improved on BIC mainly when the misspecified parameters were small, AIC did better than the BIC family when they were small, and the criteria that include the log determinant of the information matrix, IBIC among them, did poorly.

sem_information_criteria(fit_three,
                         measures = c("AIC", "BIC", "SABIC", "HBIC",
                                      "IBIC", "SPBIC"))
term value
AIC 19198.131
BIC 19275.980
SABIC 19209.380
HBIC 19237.384
IBIC 19116.779
SPBIC 19257.426
log_likelihood -9578.065
npar 21
N 301

Smaller is preferred; only a difference between models fitted to the same data under the same likelihood is meaningful.

Log likelihood: the normal log likelihood of the complete data.

IBIC and SPBIC depend on how the latent variables are identified (here variance fixed) and on the mean structure, IBIC also on the units; compare only models that share them.

SPBIC prior: Bollen et al. (2014, p. 6): free loadings and regression coefficients centered at zero, other free parameters at their estimates; Q = 961.148, dimension 21.

A fitted model supplies ℓ\ell (lavaan’s logLik()), dd, and NN, and for IBIC and SPBIC lavaan’s expected and observed information matrices, which are per observation and are multiplied by NN. They are the matrices the criteria are defined on under lavaan’s defaults, the expected information at the fitted moments (h1.information = "structured") and the negative Hessian (observed.information = "hessian"). Fits with other settings are refused for these two criteria, as are robust (MLM, MLR) fits, since both criteria rest on the normal theory information that a robust fit was chosen not to trust, and fits with several groups, equality constraints, missing data, exploratory (rotated) blocks, or fixed.x = TRUE with exogenous observed variables. The default prior of SPBIC follows Bollen et al. (2014, p. 6): free loadings and regression coefficients are centered at zero and every other free parameter at its estimate, and the footer reports the resulting QQ. The function refuses a fit whose fit function is not a log likelihood (ordered indicators, an estimator other than ML or its robust variants, which maximize the same likelihood), the Wishart likelihood, sampling weights, whose pseudo log likelihood lacks the justification of the penalties (Asparouhov, 2005), and for the BIC family a two-level model, whose sample size in the penalty is ambiguous; AIC remains available for it.

Units and Identification

AIC, BIC, SABIC, and HBIC depend on a model only through ℓ\ell and dd, which do not change when an observed variable is rescaled or a latent variable is identified another way. IBIC and SPBIC also depend on the information matrix in the free parameters as they are parameterized. IBIC keeps log⁡|𝐈‾E|\log|\bar{\mathbf I}_E| but drops the prior density, which is the term whose Jacobian would cancel a change of parameterization. When the units of a free parameter are multiplied by ckc^k, log⁡|𝐈‾E|\log|\bar{\mathbf I}_E| changes by −2klog⁡c-2k\log c, so rescaling one observed variable changes the IBIC of one model relative to another by that amount for each free parameter the first has and the second lacks that carries the variable’s units.

Adding the residual covariance of visual perception and lozenges to the three-factor model shows the consequence. The difference of each criterion (the model with the covariance less the model without it) is computed with the tests in their original units and with every test standardized, a choice some analysts make to put the variables on a common scale.

with_covariance <- paste(three, "t1_visual_perception ~~ t4_lozenges",
                         sep = "\n")
criteria <- c("BIC", "HBIC", "IBIC", "SPBIC")
difference <- function(data) {
  without <- lavaan::cfa(three, data = data, std.lv = TRUE)
  with <- lavaan::cfa(with_covariance, data = data, std.lv = TRUE)
  v(sem_information_criteria(with, measures = criteria), criteria) -
    v(sem_information_criteria(without, measures = criteria), criteria)
}
standardized <- holzinger_swineford
standardized[tests] <- scale(standardized[tests])
units <- rbind(original_units = difference(holzinger_swineford),
               standardized = difference(standardized))
colnames(units) <- criteria
units
#>                     BIC     HBIC      IBIC    SPBIC
#> original_units 4.679142 2.841265 -6.736539 6.058919
#> standardized   4.679142 2.841265  1.561660 6.058968

# The change in the IBIC difference, and twice the log of the product of
# the standard deviations of the two tests the added covariance joins.
ibic_change <- units["standardized", "IBIC"] - units["original_units", "IBIC"]
log_units <- 2 * log(prod(d$sd[match(c("t1_visual_perception", "t4_lozenges"),
                                     d$variable)]))
c(ibic_change = ibic_change, log_units = log_units)
#> ibic_change   log_units 
#>    8.298199    8.298183

BIC, HBIC, and SPBIC give the same difference either way (SPBIC up to the convergence tolerance of the fits), and all three favor the model without the covariance. IBIC favors the model with it in the original units (-6.74) and the model without it once the tests are standardized (1.56). The change, 8.30, is 2log⁡(s1s4)2\log(s_1s_4) = 8.30 (up to the convergence tolerance of the fits) for the standard deviations s1s_1 and s4s_4 of the two tests, because the one parameter the second model adds, the residual covariance, carries the units of both; every other parameter is shared by the two models, and its contribution cancels. Neither choice of units is the correct one; an IBIC comparison is defined only for a stated choice, which a report should give, and IBIC is best read beside BIC, HBIC, and SPBIC. The QQ of SPBIC is unchanged by a linear rescaling when the prior mean is transformed with the estimates, which the default prior does. Identification matters to both criteria: fixing the factor variances (std.lv = TRUE) or a marker loading are related by a nonlinear map whose Jacobian differs between models, and under the default prior of SPBIC a free loading is centered at zero while a factor variance stays at its estimate. A mean structure adds the saturated means to dd and their information to 𝐈‾E\bar{\mathbf I}_E, so it matters too. The footer of sem_information_criteria() names the identification, and compare_sem() refuses models that differ in their mean structure or, when the criterion is IBIC or SPBIC under its default prior, in how they identify their latent variables.

Relative to the Saturated Model

Bollen et al. (2014) report each criterion of a model as its difference from the criterion of the saturated model, so that BIC becomes T−dflog⁡NT-df\log N (their Eq. 12) and HBIC T−dflog⁡{N/(2π)}T-df\log\{N/(2\pi)\} (their Eq. 15). Their Table 6 compares five models of family income for N=3912N=3912 respondents, and every row can be rebuilt from the quantities the table prints.

T_ml <- c(534.27, 412.93, 26.26, 62.44, 203.33)
df_ml <- c(6, 10, 3, 6, 7)
N_ml <- 3912
logdet_model <- c(102.61, 74.26, 130.18, 102.77, 94.19)
logdet_saturated <- 134.89
Q_model <- c(1137006314, 180774515, 214642815, 251962808, 189536063)
Q_saturated <- 195428707
spbic_penalty <- function(Q, d) ifelse(Q > d, d * (1 + log(Q / d)), Q)
table_six <- data.frame(
  model = c("autoregressive", "latent growth curve", "ALT, rho free",
            "ALT, rho equal", "ALT, rho zero"),
  BIC = T_ml - df_ml * log(N_ml),
  HBIC = T_ml - df_ml * log(N_ml / (2 * pi)),
  IBIC = T_ml - df_ml * log(N_ml / (2 * pi)) - logdet_saturated + logdet_model,
  SPBIC = T_ml + spbic_penalty(Q_model, c(9, 3, 10, 7, 6)) -
    spbic_penalty(Q_saturated, 15))
table_six
#>                 model        BIC       HBIC       IBIC     SPBIC
#> 1      autoregressive 484.639176 495.666438 463.386438 450.42012
#> 2 latent growth curve 330.211960 348.590730 287.960730 208.93261
#> 3       ALT, rho free   1.444588   6.958219   2.248219 -55.66083
#> 4      ALT, rho equal  12.809176  23.836438  -8.283562 -69.50767
#> 5       ALT, rho zero 145.427372 158.292511 117.592511  52.20014

The IBIC column follows their Eq. 17, in which the log determinants are of the information per observation. Their SPBIC row uses smaller parameter counts than the full ones, printed in parentheses (15 for the saturated model rather than 20), and the table states no rule for them; sem_information_criteria() uses all the free parameters by default, and its spbic_dimension argument exists to reproduce such a table, never to tune a ranking. The rebuilt values match the printed ones to rounding. They also show that the smallest SPBIC in the table belongs to the ALT model with equal autoregressive parameters (-69.51), whereas the article’s text and its marker of the best model point to the ALT model with free parameters (-55.66). The rebuilt arithmetic agrees with the printed numbers, so the disagreement lies between the table and its reading, not in the computation.

Ranking Candidate Models

compare_sem() ranks a named list of fitted models by one criterion, BIC by default. A one-factor model, in which a single general ability accounts for all nine tests, joins the two models above.

one <- paste("general =~", paste(tests, collapse = " + "))
fit_one <- lavaan::cfa(one, data = holzinger_swineford, std.lv = TRUE)
candidates <- list(one_factor = fit_one, three_factor = fit_three,
                   cross_loading = fit_cross)
by_bic <- compare_sem(candidates)
by_bic
term value delta relative_weight log_evidence_best_over_model npar
cross_loading 19248.764 0.000 1.000 0.000 22
three_factor 19275.980 27.216 0.000 13.608 21
one_factor 19485.817 237.054 0.000 118.527 18

Criterion: BIC (smaller is preferred); N = 301; 3 models.

Checked: the same cases and data values, observed variables, missing data method (missing = “listwise”), and mean structure (meanstructure = FALSE); no exogenous variables conditioned on.

relative_weight: approximate posterior probability of each model within this set under equal prior odds; log_evidence_best_over_model: approximate log Bayes factor of the best model over each.

For model kk, Δk=Ck−min⁡jCj\Delta_k=C_k-\min_j C_j (column delta), and its relative weight is exp⁡(−Δk/2)/∑jexp⁡(−Δj/2)\exp(-\Delta_k/2)/\sum_j\exp(-\Delta_j/2). For BIC, HBIC, IBIC, and SPBIC, exp⁡(−Δk/2)\exp(-\Delta_k/2) approximates the Bayes factor of model kk against the best model, the weights approximate the posterior probabilities of the models when each has the same prior probability, and Δk/2\Delta_k/2 approximates the log Bayes factor of the best model over model kk (Bollen et al., 2012; Burnham & Anderson, 2004). For AIC the weights are Akaike weights, the weight of evidence that a model is the one in the set closest to the data generating process in Kullback-Leibler discrepancy (Burnham & Anderson, 2004), and SABIC approximates no marginal likelihood; for both the log evidence column is NA.

The cross-loading model is preferred by a wide margin. Its BIC is smaller than that of the three-factor model by 27.22, an approximate log Bayes factor of 13.61, and smaller than that of the one-factor model by 237.05. SPBIC gives differences of 27.79 and 230.32 and AIC 30.92 and 251.88, with the same order. The two three-factor models are nested, so the cross-loading can also be tested by the difference of their statistics:

lrt <- v(fit_measures, "chi_square") - v(cross_measures, "chi_square")
lrt_df <- v(fit_measures, "df") - v(cross_measures, "df")
lrt_p <- pchisq(lrt, lrt_df, lower.tail = FALSE)

The test agrees, χ2\chi^2(1) = 32.92, pp < 0.0001.

The weights are conditional on the set: adding or removing a model changes all of them. They say which model the data favor among those compared, not how well any of them fits, which the measures of the earlier sections address; the best model in a set can fit poorly. Nor do they carry the sampling variability of the criteria, so the uncertainty of the selection itself is not estimated.

What Is Checked Before Comparing

A criterion compares models only through their log likelihoods, so compare_sem() first checks that the log likelihoods are comparable and refuses, naming the two models and what differs, when they are not:

  • the same cases and data values (or, for models fitted to summary statistics, the same sample moments), the same observed variables in any order, and the same groups, since a log likelihood is a density of the variables and cases it models;
  • the same missing data method, since listwise deletion, FIML, and the two-stage method give different likelihoods;
  • the same mean structure, since without one lavaan leaves the saturated means out of the parameter count;
  • the same exogenous observed variables when fixed.x or conditional.x is TRUE, since lavaan’s log likelihood is then conditional on them, and two saturated models of the same three variables that condition on different ones differ by hundreds of BIC points (refit every model with fixed.x = FALSE);
  • a likelihood the criteria are defined on: ML or its robust variants, the normal likelihood, no sampling weights, no ordered indicators;
  • for IBIC, and for SPBIC under its default prior, one identification for every latent variable of every model: each by a marker indicator, or each by a fixed variance (a set that uses both is refused, also when every model mixes them in the same way).

A model identified by marker indicators (lavaan’s default) cannot be ranked by IBIC against the models above, which fix the factor variances:

fit_three_marker <- lavaan::cfa(three, data = holzinger_swineford)
compare_sem(list(marker = fit_three_marker, cross_loading = fit_cross),
            criterion = "IBIC")
#> Error:
#> ! IBIC depends on how the latent variables are identified, so compare_sem() requires every latent variable of every model to be identified the same way, and these models use more than one identification (fits$marker: marker indicator; fits$cross_loading: variance fixed). Refit every model with one identification: std.lv = TRUE for all (each latent variance fixed at 1) or the marker indicator for all (lavaan's default).

The check cannot establish that the models are scientifically comparable, or that a prior is sensible; it establishes only that the criterion is defined for the comparison.

The Expected Cross-Validation Index

The expected cross-validation index of Browne and Cudeck (1989) estimates the discrepancy a fitted model would show in an independent sample of the same size from the same population, ECVÎ=F̂+2d/a=(T+2d)/a\widehat{ECVI}=\hat F+2d/a=(T+2d)/a (their Eq. 5), and ecvi() reports it with an interval that replaces T−dfT-df by the noncentrality limits. When TT is the likelihood ratio statistic, N⋅ECVÎ=AIC+2ℓsN\cdot\widehat{ECVI}=AIC+2\ell_s for the saturated log likelihood ℓs\ell_s, so ECVI and AIC rank models fitted to the same data identically; the value of the ECVI is a discrepancy per observation, with an interval.

ecvi_values <- t(sapply(candidates, function(fit)
  v(ecvi(fit, conf_level = 0.90), c("ecvi", "ci_lower", "ci_upper"))))
colnames(ecvi_values) <- c("ecvi", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")
ecvi_values
#>                    ecvi  ci_lower  ci_upper
#> one_factor    1.1570238 0.9803526 1.3584808
#> three_factor  0.4229419 0.3416835 0.5294137
#> cross_loading 0.3202064 0.2627798 0.4032658

The order is that of AIC. The point estimate is not truncated, so for a model with T<dfT<df it falls below the lower limit of its interval, whose noncentrality cannot be negative. A difference between two ECVIs, like a difference between two RMSEAs or CFIs, is not bounded by the limits of the separate intervals; an interval for such a difference needs the joint sampling distribution of the two, which Lai (2020) derives for differences in RMSEA and CFI between nested or nonnested models.

Reporting the Analysis

A results paragraph assembled from the tables above might read:

The three-factor model of Jöreskog (1969) did not fit the nine tests exactly, χ2\chi^2(24) = 85.31, pp < 0.0001, NN = 301. The estimated RMSEA was 0.092, 90% CI [0.071, 0.114], and the unbiased SRMR 0.058, 90% CI [0.042, 0.074]; CFI was 0.931 against the independence model. The standardized residuals showed the straight and curved capitals test sharing more covariance with the three visual tests than the model implied. Allowing that test to load on the visual factor, a modification suggested by these data, reduced the RMSEA to 0.065, 90% CI [0.042, 0.089], and the unbiased SRMR to 0.035, 90% CI [0.020, 0.049], and was preferred by BIC over the three-factor model (Δ\DeltaBIC = 27.22) and over a one-factor model (Δ\DeltaBIC = 237.05). Fit within an RMSEA of .08, the tolerance set before the analysis, was not established for either model; the data endorse fit within 0.089 for the modified model.

What Global Fit Does Not Settle

  • Where the misfit is. A single index averages over every moment the model reproduces. The residuals, read alongside the indices, locate it.
  • The structural part. In a model with latent regressions, the substantive question is usually the fit of the structural relations, and an index that lumps the measurement and structural parts together does not answer it directly (Lai, 2024). Lai (2024) and Zhang and Wu (2024) develop estimates, intervals, and tests for the fit of the structural part; the functions here evaluate the whole model.
  • Differences in fit between models. A sample difference in RMSEA or CFI can be smaller than, larger than, or of opposite sign to the population difference (Lai, 2020), and the limits of two separate intervals do not bound it.
  • Improper solutions and multilevel models. A fit that did not converge, or whose solution lavaan’s post-estimation check flags as improper (a negative variance estimate, or a covariance matrix of the latent variables, of the residuals, or of the structural residuals that is not positive definite), is refused, since its fit measures describe estimates outside the parameter space. With auxiliary variables the check is made on the model’s own parameters: lavaan’s own check also tests the residual covariances of the auxiliary variables, which are not positive definite once an auxiliary variable is related to a factor strongly enough, however proper the model’s solution. A multilevel fit is refused by sem_fit_measures(), since one set of indices mixes the levels; lavaan’s level specific fit measures are the tool for it.
  • Cutoffs. No value of any index certifies a model. The intervals and the tests of close and not close fit say how precisely the data locate the misfit, and a tolerance chosen in advance turns that into a decision.
